text_fidelity_a:
Ring Video Doorbell 2 with HD Video, Motion Activated Alerts, Easy Installation Another reviewer mentioned these issues, but I was impulsive and bought it anyways. They are all true.
- I spend a good deal of time adjusting the sensibility settings and using the brackets (both V and H) to reduce false positives, but they are still too many. My door is about 25-30' from the road and if a truck passes, even small cars, "motion detected". You stop giving importance for the sensor.
- I try to answer motion but it takes so long to load (I have an S8, with good wifi) and I got a connection problem way too often. If wasn't another false positive (as usually is), I would have missed the person lurking.
- The recording starts too late. when you go see the recorded video (because you were not able to answer the false positive motion), the video starts way too long after the movement started.
- regarding payments: I have a Piper camera that records up to 1,000 24s videos for free, overwriting after that. It works great. It always worked. Why Ring enforce additional payment is mind-blowing considering what is available on the market.
- I have installed with battery, that was really good because it was easy to install, but on the current pace (75% after 25 days) there is no way it will last the suggested 6 months on the website.

UPDATE: had to completely disable the motion sensor, the false positives were driving me crazy. Not paying the monthly fee. It's too many clicks to get to the screen when somebody actually pushes the button.
Avoid this product and wait for competitors to come up with something better.
UPDATE 2: Now this piece of crap will not enter live view.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell 2 with HD Video, Motion Activated Alerts, Easy Installation

text_fidelity_a:
Ubiquiti Networks Unifi 802.11ac Dual-Radio PRO Access Point (UAP-AC-PRO-US), Single,White I purchased two of these and their Cloud Key (CK). They come with good mounts but are attractive enough to just sit on a book case or shelf. The blue LED is a bit intrusive if installing in a dark room like a home theater, BUT using the CK, selecting the AP, then Configuration, you can disable it. Using the CK, the installation of new firmware, network configuration, general setup took less than an hour. The bulk of the time was doing the firmware updates and smoke testing.

My home is not big, 1500 sq. ft., but the 5G versus the 2.5 has a relatively small signal radius so I went with two at opposite sides of the house. If you want to benefit with the higher speeds plan accordingly. Meshing the two APs was painless and in my opinion requires little to no networking knowledge using the CK or downloading and installing their software. The CK is optional.

So far, no drops or sudden slow downs. Just solid performance. The unit today costs $130 USD. A great value for enterprise features and the option to integrate and provide further features with other Unifi products.
text_fidelity_b: Ubiquiti Networks Unifi 802.11ac Dual-Radio PRO Access Point (UAP-AC-PRO-US), Single,White

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th) I've been an avid fan of ebooks since the long gone days of the Rocket and the eBookman, and a fan of the Kindle since the very beginning. This is miles and away the best there has ever been. It is a luxury model, no doubt, but oh is it luxurious.

I like:
The weight. Even in the case it's very light, though if it gets much lighter I'll worry about it blowing away in a strong wind.
The size. It's not going to get much smaller without shrinking the screen.
The interface. I'm sorry, I like buttons. Call me old. I never bent back the spine of a book (horrors) so I can't compare the feel of this to that, but I can say it's nice for a long reading session. The touch screen takes a bit of getting used to, but the tutorial will guide a new user. The tutorial is intrusive at first, but provides useful information and goes away quickly. I will suggest customizing the screen. I hated the default, but you get a lot of options to make it just the way you want.
The lighting is now all but invisible. I was unhappy that you can't completely turn it off as you could with the Nook Glowlight, and turning it down casts an odd yellow light over the page, but it's so even now as to be so unintrusive I barely notice going from sunlight to tunnel on the bus home. With the Nook I'd be thrown out of the book to go turn on the light. With the Kindle, I can keep reading without a pause. It does not have adaptive lighting, but I'm not sure it needs it.
The download speed. I don't know if it's supposed to be faster than the Kindle Keyboard (the last one I had with 3G) but it certainly seems that way.
The battery life. Maybe with this thing going for months we'll finally hear an end to the "but my dead tree doesn't run out of power" nonsense.
Next in series. When you're almost done with a book, it tells you where the story continues. Now the next feature I want, and if it does this I haven't seen it yet, is an alert when the next book in a series I'm following is published. Yes, FictFact is great, but I'm greedy and want it right on the device.

I don't like:
It's not waterproof. There was a lot of hope it would be after the Nook went that route.
It's not solar, yet, but there are rumors of a solar cover coming soon.
It doesn't support Audible and the excellent immersive reading between ebook and audiobook. I have a weird love of that feature, seeing what changed print to audio.
Recommended Content and Reading Lists. I shut this feature off. The information seems scattered at best and gave me no useful information, especially considering how precious screen real estate is.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th)

Fire HD 10 Tablet with Alexa, 10.1" HD Display, 16 GB, Black - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) Love it! Waited all year long to get this for Christmas. I have been owning an iPod (for music and video), a 7 inch Kindle (for books, music and video, and a laptop PC for email and everything else. Because of how much I like Amazon Prime Music and Music Unlimited, I decided to try to reduce the amount of high dollar items I need to replace every 3 to 4 years. So I am attempting to use the 10 inch Kindle to replace both the iPod and PC laptop.

So far so good. Email is easy to use. I have loaded the HP ePrint app to be able to print out bills I pay online, etc for records. Having the music available on any device is wonderful. I also have a 7 inch Kindle HDX my wife uses and access the music on my Android Smartphone as well.

The Kindle HD 10 has a wonderful picture. Nice to be able to use the Xfinity app to watch shows off my DVR, like Atlanta Hawks games while my wife watches something else on the large tv. Much better than watching on my 5 inch smartphone screen.

The audio is good and if I want to play it louder can send it over to one of my bluetooth speakers. I use the bluetooth keyboard and love it. That is what allows me to replace my PC as I can type emails rather than one finger type them.

I got the 16 GB with 128 GB SD memory card. Adding the memory card slot is a big improvement over previous kindles I have.

I read graphic novels like The Walking Dead series and being able to see them easily on the 10 inch screen is also a big improvement.

I highly recommend this!

It records in user-selectable WAV or MP3 formats in various selectable bitrates. It has adjustable gain control and a noise reduction function. One important function for voice recording is the ability to monitor while recording using ear buds or headphones, and this recorder has that capability. The display screen isn't as sharp and clear as it is portrayed in the listing photos, but it is decent.

Now for the minor negatives, for which I dinged a star off the review rating. One is the printing labeling the buttons on the one I received is only a little lighter than the color of the recorder, making them very hard to read. That means you have to memorize the button location and functions or keep the user manual handy for reference. And that leads to the second negative, and that is the print in the user manual is tiny. Really tiny. I looked for a PDF version online and couldn't find one. The manual suggests visiting the brand's web site, but neither the manual nor the box provide a URL. Or even the listing brand name (Tenmatec) for that matter. I wound taking photographs of the manual pages with a tablet so I could enlarge them for easier reading. The other minor negative is that it has no USB-C port, only a micro USB for recharging or connecting to a computer for moving files around.

Other than that it's a good recorder. It has one-button functionality (although there is a slight delay when starting a recording while it starts up). Because of its metal construction and heft it feels good in-hand and looks really good.
text_fidelity_b: TenmaTec Voice Recorder with Playback,80GB Voice Activated Recorder with DSP Noise Reduction,Dual Microphones, Mp3,Speaker,Password Protect,for Music,Overdubbing,Studio,Dictation,Interview

SPARIN Galaxy Tab S3 / Galaxy Tab S2 9.7 Screen Protector - S Pen Compatible / Tempered Glass / 2.5D Round Edge / Scratch Resistant / Easy Install for Samsung Galaxy Tab S3 / Galaxy Tab S2 9.7 Inch Crystal clear, fits well, and is very light weight. Honestly, I was a little nervous about buying what I perceived to be a cheaper product online. However, the idea of paying 40+ dollars to have a screen protector applied to my screens always seemed outrageous to me. So I figured I'd give it a shot and after reading the reviews for several products, I decided to give this Sparin a shot and ordered one for my Galaxy Tab S2.

Placing the screen protector on the S2 was painless and quick. A few quick wipes with the wet and dry clothes provided and a few moments centering the screen protector over the tablet screen. Put the stickers on to hold the screen protector in place, peel off the backing, and put it on the screen. No joke, it's pretty simple. So simple that I managed to somehow mess it up.

What resulted in me messing the up install and quickly attempting to fix is soon resulted in two corners that would not stay down. "No problem," I though, since the screen protector is designed to be re-applied several times. However, after one or two attempts, and with now two corner sticking up, I was resigned to having a screen protector that just sticks up.

As a last resort, I contacted Sparin support. Despite a small hiccup with email addresses, I quickly heard back from support. They provided a few useful tips to apply the screen protector and to attempt to get the corners to stay down. Ultimately, the tips did not work. Again, I was going to be stuck with a screen protector that sticks up.

Not so! As it turns out. Sparin did not hesitate to send me another screen protector. No questions asked. No photos requested. Not subject to verification. Just a quick reply from Sparin apologizing for a bad experience (which I will admit is mostly my fault), and that a replacement was already in the mail - it is! - and with that, they earned a very loyal customer.

I cannot say the product is poor, because it's not. I have no doubt this protector will keep my screen free of scratches. However, my attempts to install it were lackluster. There's a reason we paid trained teenagers at the mall to install these things for us.

Luckily for me, this great product is backed up with amazing support.

text_fidelity_a:
Sony UBP-X800 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray Player Picture is nice,

The real reason I'm sending the units (I've had two) back, however, is that the player refuses to output the various high quality audio formats, including 7.1 DTS Master Audio. The digital coax cable barely works and the HDMI 2 audio output simply does not work, Admittedly I have an older receiver -- a Sony STR-DA5400ES, from 2009. But it has multiple HDMI inputs and the HDMI 2 audio output on the X800 is specifically designed to send audio to an older amp. Even Sony phone support says it should work. But it doesn't.. I spent 1 hour and 7 minutes with Sony ES support today going through every possible menu permutation on both the Amp and the UBP-X800 player. No luck The HDMI is dead. Zero output. The coax output can only send DTS EX 5.1, even though the player itself tells me it's playing DTS Master Audio 7.1.

This UBP-X800 has two HDMI outputs: one for video, one for audio. In case you don't have a 4K receiver with the ever-changing HDMI protocols, you're supposed to be able to feed HDMI audio to the amp. So I fed the video directly to the Samsung's video input (a direct cable connection) and another HDMI to my amp.

Zero audio from the player's HDMI audio feed. Not a peep of audio at all.

So I used the orange RCA digital audio coax connector to get surround sound audio.

But the coax digital audio cable only delivers DTS EX 5.1, not the 7.1 DTS Master Audio available on the Kingsman 4K disk. I updated the player's and the TV's firmware and read the manual. Nothing fixes the problem. Using all new, very short, high-speed HDMI 2.0 cables too.

My ancient Sony BDP-S560 Blu-ray player feeds all formats to the same 5400ES amp properly. I get great 7.1 DTS Master HD audio. Thus my old Blu-ray player sounds way better than my brand new advanced Sony UHD player.
Researching at the Sony forum under the UBP-X800 Audio Problems thread, answers were all over the place and none worked, I tried to register so I could post my problem and the website wouldn't allow me to. The comments there were complaining that they could not get the ATMOS tracks working.

I have no choice but to pack both X800s up and send them back.

Eventually I found that I needed to plug the 4K player into input 3 of the TV for the image to stabilize. Interesting that only some inputs on the TV can handle UHD source. But still, the player's audio doesn't work with my Sony Amp (Sony's fault).

HDMI was supposed to solve all these problems, but I suspect the HDCP copy protection schemes are really screwing things up or the firmware has bugs or companies just produce inferior products. Rather disappointing.
text_fidelity_b: Sony UBP-X800 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray Player

First of all, it is huge! Second, it comes with a 10-inch tabletop or floor level light ring with its own stand. Of course, there are the two remotes and an app you can use to take photos and set your light levels with.

I'm an amateur at using ring lights for my photo taking, and this one is no piece of cake to set up. The instructions are terrible for someone who is usually pretty good at following them. and the remote and app take some playing around with to figure them out. Also, the remote does not automatically pair with your phone the next time you want to use it, so you have to pair them over again. This is a bit annoying.

I have a Note 10+ with a case and it barely fits into the holder. I'm so glad it does. The whole setup feels nice and sturdy all the way around, from the bottom of the stand to phone holders. I sell bulk bought makeup online, and it's nice to have a ring big enough that it doesn't show up on the surface of the shiny palettes. I can place it so there are no shadows or bright spots, and the light is up far enough that it is not in my way. It is that big. I am working with four to six inch items, so that helps, too. It makes my life so much easier.

The ten inch ring light is great for getting perfect shoe photos. I love buying shoes, and always take photos to put on the end of the boxes, so I can see exactly what I have at a glance. It makes picking out my shoes for the day easy, when I can see the actual shoe, and not a drawing of it.

These lights are the best I've bought. They are made very well, and so is everything they come with. You will not find a better setup at a better cost. A beginner or novice will have everything you need to start taking photos or videos right out of the box. You may, however, find better instructions on how to put a setup together in a different set, but then you wouldn't get half the amount or half the quality of the items you get in this one. It may take some trial and error, but if I can figure out how to set this up, I'm pretty sure anyone can. I have cognitive difficulties and things don't come easy. It took me a good while and I did ask for some help with one thing from my son, but I got it done, and it was worth the trouble. 4 stars ✨
text_fidelity_b: E EyeGrab 14'' Studio Selfie Ring Light with 94'' Tripod Stand, Adjustable 3000K-7000K Color Temperature Lighting for YTB Portrait Photo Video, Camera Phone Laptop, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Zinwell ZAT-970A Digital to Analog TV Converter Box (for Antenna Use) We needed to save some money, and I'd heard that Over The Air broadcasts included channels you wouldn't otherwise get. My Dish TV account provided local channels and a whole bunch of channels I didn't use; but the OTA feature really helps!

I paired the Zinwell digital / analog converter box (highly rated, outstanding Amazon price) with the Radio Shack Antennacraft® HDX1000 Amplified HDTV Antenna (also highly rated). You should know one thing -- the mast size for the Dish TV is larger than the mast size for the Antennacraft antenna, so you can't just remove the Dish and replace it with the Antennacraft on the same mast. But it is an easy install.

As a trial, before going up to the roof (2 story house), I set the Antennacraft in the downstairs window that has a view to the southwest (the direction our local TV stations broadcast from). Without the Zinwell, you're limited to the low power analog stations (mostly Spanish language, a few home shopping stations). I think I got about 6 stations. Then I plugged in the Zinwell in line between the antenna and the TV (after disconnecting the Dish TV feed), did a scan, and had 20 channels. Repeated the process upstairs (remember, we have a 2 story) and had 22 channels!! All the local tv stations (NBC, ABC, CW, ION, PBS, etc.) that broadcast digitally came through great!! Unfortunately, it started raining :( so after the rain stopped, I only got as far as getting the mast installed outdoors before it got too dark. It won't take long to finish.

Only one Zinwell related item: You're supposed to be able to choose the feed from the Zinwell to the TV to be either Coax or the Composite (yellow video, red and white audio). I couldn't get the composite to work in setup, but the coax worked just fine. Haven't had a chance to see if, once programmed, the composite would work, or if for some reason I hooked it up to my tv incorrectly (hard to imagine), but ... since the coax works so well, and video and audio quality are great, I'm money ahead and not complaining!!

So when do I break even? $80 antenna plus 2 $40 boxes = $160; Dish TV was costing me about $55/month (yeah, once you've been a subscriber for a while, there's essentially no customer retention policy, so, good by Dish!! -- and that's probably true for Directv and Comcast, too). So after 3 months, essentially at the start of January, I'm home free!! Thanks, Amazon, you're helping me save money, and that's really great!!

NOTE: I only ordered one Zinwell to test out things, now I've ordered a second for our other TV (didn't want to put too much at risk if it didn't work, but it works great!).

NOTE 2: The gov't coupon program is long dead, no hope of getting $40 off on one, just be glad if you waited that these things are as reasonably priced as they are.
text_fidelity_b: Zinwell ZAT-970A Digital to Analog TV Converter Box (for Antenna Use)

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Harmony 950 Touch IR Remote Control - Discontinued by Manufacturer Logitech makes the best universal remote controls and they keep introducing new models that are better and better. If you have half a dozen (or more) remote controls on your living room table and are always losing some of them or forgetting which does what, then a universal remote is for you.

The Harmony 950 appears to be mostly the same as the Harmony Elite, except without the Harmony Hub device. The Harmony Hub can be purchased separately later, though the Elite package is cheaper if you're getting it anyway. The Harmony Hub greatly expands the range and capabilities of your Harmony remote, so you should think twice before skipping it.

Logitech also sells much cheaper Harmony remotes without the touch screen. The main benefit of the touch screen is to program shortcuts to your favorite TV channels and to control more devices than the non-touch remote controls can access. If you always use your DVR or cable box's on-screen channel menu and only have a few devices, then maybe a much cheaper Harmony without the touch screen is a better value for you.

The Harmony is pretty easy to program by connecting to your PC and connecting to the Logitech website. If you have an older Harmony remote, you may be able to transfer all your device settings to this one. The buttons on the Harmony are easy to see, well spaced and give you good feedback when pressed.

Battery life is OK for a touchscreen device, but like your smartphone you will need to recharge this at least every couple of days. Most people will leave the Harmony in the recharging station most of the time, so make sure you have an electrical outlet close to where you will be using the Harmony.

If you're in the market for a universal remote, Logitech Harmony should be first on your list. The only decision you have to make is which model to buy. If you're trying to control a handful of devices (TV, cable box, DVR, stereo system, game system, DVD player), then you really have to ask yourself if the touchscreen feature is worth the big price premium. If you have a "smart home" with remote controlled lights, outlets, thermostat, etc or if your devices are spread around a large room so the IR remote has trouble connecting with them, then the Harmony Hub is a good idea.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Harmony 950 Touch IR Remote Control - Discontinued by Manufacturer

text_fidelity_a:
co2CREA Hard Case with Sleep Mode Replacement for Apple AirPods Max Headphone (Black Case + Inside Red) This is a smart case - no bra needed.

UPDATE: Wrong, alas. I mean, it’s possible to make this case put your headphones to sleep – at least with the version of this case that I have – but it’s such a precise, finicky, painstaking endeavor that it’s nowhere near worth the effort. I’ve taken to using my case just like everybody else does: with the bra inside.

My guess is that what these third-party case makers need to do is what Apple did with the bra: rather than a couple of dime-sized round magnets, they need to put in long, thin magnets that will connect with the sensors in the earcups no matter where in the case they fall. The bra puts the headphones to sleep every time without fail and without the user having to spend several minutes massaging the headphones into just exactly the perfect position so that they’ll go to sleep, so it can be done; the third-party case manufacturers just haven’t yet figured out how Apple did it.

Anyways: I was dreading this case having an horrendous stench to it, based on several reviews I've read. I'm happy to report that while mine has a smell and it is kind of chemical-y, I find the smell neither strong nor entirely unpleasant. It's pretty mild, strength-wise (and I'm sensitive to such things) and I find the smell has a sort of fresh quality to it, despite its chemical nature. Lucky me, I guess. But this, like the Apple bra, is basically half a case. You need the bra to put the headphones to sleep, and this case to give them adequate protection. Hard to believe in this day and age, but there it is. I guess if Apple included a case with these that did everything necessary they would probably charge an additional $200 for it…
text_fidelity_b: co2CREA Hard Case with Sleep Mode Replacement for Apple AirPods Max Headphone (Black Case + Inside Red)

LeadsaiL Wireless Computer Mouse, 2.4G Portable Slim Cordless Mouse Less Noise for Laptop Optical Mouse with 4 Buttons, AA Battery Used, USB Mouse for Laptop, Desktop, MacBook Great shape, very much like the classic and ubiquitous Logitech. I like that the pairing device is on-board. Lightweight and simple, a mouse is important for me if needing to get serious work done, especially anything with CAD or Visio.

The big question you need to ask yourself is, do you want a Bluetooth version or one like this that has its own receiver. It seems to me that if you always use this with the same computer and you have Bluetooth built in to the computer, then you probably want Bluetooth. Conversely, if you want this to use with multiple computers and/or you don't have Bluetooth built in to any one of the computers you will use the mouse with, then you'd want something like this. This is because pairing is easier in a case such as this, and drivers usually aren't an issue. Bluetooth usually isn't an issue either, but it might get irritating with frequent changing of machines. At least that is my experience.

Does not come with a carry bag, surprisingly. Mouse roller also functions as a button, as it should. It has an on/off switch on the back, which is nice for saving battery life and being able to leave this hooked up to a permanent install (although with a permanent desk setup, I personally stick with wired).

I particularly like that it works with Android (at least on phones that support USB OTG, which is most these days). It would have been even better if the Bluetooth worked with Android, but at least with my Pixel 4, it didn't.

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th) “I wonder how long it has been we readers have gazed at the young person sitting under a tree at night reading a book on the Kindle home screen..oh, our love affair with books and being able to read our stories late into the night…...by candlelight….anywhere.”

Pre-release technology reviewers commenting on the price of the Kindle Oasis are wrong. The new Kindle Oasis is worth the the price Amazon is charging, including cover it hardly represents at all an increase in price when compared with a Kindle Voyage with cover. Yet it provides the two most asked for improvements in mobile devices: increased battery life reducing the need to frequently recharge, and improved screen legibility (new sans-serif Ember font, and more LEDS that provide increased brightness).

“When we are immersed into the story of our favorite books, only that world matters.”

Pre-release technology reviewers have compared the Kindle as a single purpose e-reader, to multipurpose devices like in smartphones, tablets and computers. When we choose to read, we are seeking a bit of solitude in the day and night. Oh, how easy it is to remember being annoyed with yet another incoming phone call, text message or email. The power of focus!

“The tactile feel of a book”

Pre-release technology reviewer have labelled the Kindle as luxurious with it’s leather cover. How soon we forget our books covered with leather! And we are willing to pay an extra price for it!

As I sit across the street from the one and only Amazon retail store “in the world”, I have unboxed and set up my new Kindle Oasis. Maybe I am one of the few ordinary people outside of Amazon and the technology press in the world to have been able to purchase one so soon. The feeling reminds me of going to a release party in the same shopping center for the latest Harry Potter novel.

This Kindle is new, like the latest release from our favorite author.

It connects me to reading anywhere, late at night when there is little light.

The Kindle Oasis is magical.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th)

text_fidelity_a:
Plantronics 211856-99 Backbeat Fit 3100 True Wireless Earbuds, Sweatproof and Waterproof In Ear Workout Headphones, Grey There are "true wireless" earbuds on Amazon for half of this price, but I have tried several of them and they all suffer from poor-to-mediocre sound quality as well as poor battery life. These Plantronics earbuds cost more, but they have great sound quality as well as great battery life. I hear a good amount of bass as well as good clarity in the higher frequencies. My favorite music sounds muddy on cheaper wireless earbuds, but sounds great on these. 5 hour battery life per charge is almost double what the cheap earbuds give me. The ear hooks look clunky, but they are very comfortable and never fall off when I'm jogging or working out.

As with all "true wireless" earbuds, you have to control them with a series of short and long taps on the sides of the earbuds (to change volume, skip around in your music, answer phone calls, etc). If you have a hard time remembering all those commands (as I do), you can always pull out your phone and do the same thing from there.

If you cannot afford "true wireless" earbuds at this price level, my advice is to forget the "true wireless" design and look at Bluetooth earbuds that have a wire connecting the two sides. That style is slightly uglier than "true wireless" but has much better battery life and sound quality for similar price levels and there are pretty good products for much cheaper prices than the "true wireless" design.

I see some review complaints about connectivity and charging problems. My earbuds have worked perfectly with no dropouts, etc. As with any electronic gadget, there is always the possibility of a manufacturing flaw. I would definitely return a product that did not work flawlessly.

Note that this particular Plantronics model is not noise-cancelling or noise-isolating. You will hear some background noise, which is safer if you use them when walking or working in a busy environment. Plantronics does sell noise cancelling earbuds that you could choose instead if that feature is useful and important to you.
text_fidelity_b: Plantronics 211856-99 Backbeat Fit 3100 True Wireless Earbuds, Sweatproof and Waterproof In Ear Workout Headphones, Grey

text_fidelity_a:
ASUS SRT-AC1900 AC1900 Onhub Google WiFi Router,Black Google markets this router, the second in the Onhub series, made by Asus of Taiwan. The first was made by TP-Link in Mainland China (, just "China" since the US only recognizes one China). Google emphasizes in it's marketing how the artful simple appearance of the routers enable them to be placed on a table or shelf in your room much as you would any decorative object. Google succeeds in that objective. There are differences in appearances between the Asu and TP-Link. The TP-Link's cylinder flares outwards at the top where an indicator light is located. The Asus flares outward at the base where the indicator light is located. The TP-link shell is midnight blue. The Asus is black. I cannot escape seeing the shape of a nuclear plant cooling tower when looking at my Asus :)!

The experience I had setting up the router confirmed this is an easy device to manage. With the smartphone app On installed on my Nexus 5x, I touched the top of the router to start and finish the router setup process. After sey up, the Onhub app will should you a disgram of your home network, the devices connected to the network, and your netowrk's connection to the Internet.

Much ado has been made of the OnHub as a two port router. I use one for the connection to my cable modem, and one for the connection to mu Phillips Hue bridge to my LED Hue lights. Two ports is all I have ever needed at home.
text_fidelity_b: ASUS SRT-AC1900 AC1900 Onhub Google WiFi Router,Black

text_fidelity_a:
ARCTIC Breeze Pro USB Desktop Fan with 4-Port USB Hub This review covers two different models of the Arctic fan:

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>Model with USB hub:
I have been using the original ARCTIC Breeze for a while and have been very pleased with its performance, and especially pleased with how quiet it runs. The Pro model builds on that and adds a few more useful features.

Unlike the original model which had a bendable stem with a USB plug on the end, the Pro has a base so the fan can be positioned away from the USB port on the PC. The attached power cord is a little over 5 feet long, making it possible to put the fan on my desk and plug it into the PC on the floor.

The base also has 4 USB input ports, so it works as a USB hub. It has a 5V power input jack if you want to turn this into an active hub. The power adapter to do so is NOT included.

Unlike the single-speed original version, this has a knob so you can vary the speed. It's not precise, but there is a somewhat noticeable difference between low and high. It's a continually variable speed - you can turn the dial to whatever speed you like.

Best of all, it's just as quiet, if not quieter, than the original model. That's the biggest plus for me by far, since the cheap USB fans make a racket. This just makes a low-pitched hum. The build quality is solid - the base is sturdy, and the bendable arm holds its position well.

One negative: the packaging. It's in a clam shell package that is a major, major pain to open!

While it's more expensive than the original, the added benefits of being able to position it on a desk and use it as a hub makes the upgrade worth considering. Highly recommend.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>USA EDITION:
I've have (and use) a couple other Arctic USB fans and have been 100% satisfied with them. This new version (their "USA Edition") has a couple of improvements over past designs.

The base is a metal plate which increases the fan's stability when you're bending the stem to point the fan. The on/off/speed dial switch no longer has a lit LED ring around it. I never found the lit LED ring to be bothersome on the other Arctic fans, so having or not having it is not a big deal to me.

The base also does away with the USB hub connections that other models have. That's keeps the base more streamlined and allows it to have a lower profile. It also does away with the clam shell packaging, instead using a very easy to open box.

The build quality of this, like the other Arctic fans I have, is excellent. The stem is bendy by stays put where you want it; the operating sound is pretty hushed; the on/off/speed control works well. The overall design is attractive, with a red/white/blue color scheme and graphics.

It moves a surprising amount of air. No, it won't blow your hair back as a Vornado fan will, but this makes a noticeable difference in circulating air. The size makes it very easy to find a spot on your desk to position it.

While I can't speak to the long-term reliability of this as of yet, I expect it will last for some time. I have an Arctic fan similar to this that I've been using almost daily for the past 1+ years, and it still works as good as it did when new.

Looks good, works well, and easy to use. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: ARCTIC Breeze Pro USB Desktop Fan with 4-Port USB Hub

text_fidelity_a:
Jiusion Telescope Eyepiece Plossl Eyepiece 32mm with 1.25inch Filter Threaded, Astronomical Telescope Lens 50% FOV increase at this price? This is the lowest priced Plössl I've ever seen and the reason for choosing it. Curiosity.

As a physicist with a too time-consuming career to fool around with optical Garage-a-Tronics projects, it's time for fun. After >40 years, I'd guess 1/3 of my time was in electro-optical systems. My responsibilities included one of the nation's most sophisticated optical design, fabrication, and 50-200 layers of Å thickness vapor deposition coating capability (200 layers is no limit … simply the most I've seen engineered)

You have to give them credit. Chinese optics are extraordinary and have been for 20 years. Asian pricing has wholly changed the marketplace. The crazy low prices have made complex systems affordable to the mass market. Optical grinding facilities remaining in the US are confined to a handful of custom, proto-typing houses run by old-timers with a decidedly different product application than consumer use.

The Plössl eyepiece is quite expensive to manufacture given the nature of the glass, coatings, and its precisely coordinated concave and convex lenses to neutralize internal reflections.

The Plössl has tradeoffs. All optical systems do. For example, Plössl's increased FOV comes with an eye relief confined to 70–80% of focal length.

Lenses are analog. Performance is not binary. 'Lowest price' in optics might be misunderstood. Optics lots begin production targeted at a spec performance that makes a profit. A production lot will yield a normal distribution to spec. On the upper end of the distribution are a few 'blue diamonds' commanding a super premium. Theoretically, 66%, will meet the target spec. Production lots begin life as profitable, spec-centered customers. 7% would be expected to fall short of some spec performance (i.e. start 107% of what you need) … Harvard MBA's demanding perfection in all things except stock value have never come to terms with normal analog distributions in scientific endeavors.

The lenses come without ref to detail specs, so I would believe the factory is emptying the shelves of sub-spec product here. Spec fallout, in my experience, may have little or nothing to do with operator perceptions of performance.

Excellent fun.

Was my review helpful? If so, click "Helpful" so I can know. Trying hard to put integrity into reviews
text_fidelity_b: Jiusion Telescope Eyepiece Plossl Eyepiece 32mm with 1.25inch Filter Threaded, Astronomical Telescope Lens

text_fidelity_a:
Canon PowerShot SX280 12.1MP Digital Camera with 20x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom with 3-Inch LCD (Black) (OLD MODEL) Some people have had battery problems with this camera. I bought 2 extra Vivitar batteries with higher mA-h ratings than the stock Canon batteries. If you do the math, this camera can put a huge load on the microprocessor when you ask it to take high-rate, high-resolution videos, or multiple shots. Zoom a lot at the same time, and these little batteries aren't going to hack it. In addition, Canon has something wrong (I suspect) with the battery life sensor/indicator. (My guess is the 1.0.2.0 firmware update that's available from Canon is to help that.) On the good side, that's depressed the price of this camera. Since I don't intend to take a lot of videos with this camera, I'm OK with that. :)

I may have also gotten a good one. Over 2 days of playing with it, I've yet to change the battery. It's showing 2/3 charge. It has however, flashed "charge the battery" warnings a
couple of times.

For calibration, this is replacing a Canon A1100IS we bought about 4 years ago as a second camera.

Pro (for me):
Really good, clear pictures
Good image stabilization (hand-holding at 1/15th of a second or slower!)
Low noise, as low as ISO 1600
Large zoom range
Manual focus
DIGIC 6 processor (latest generation)
Very nice screen
P, Av, Tv & M exposure modes
Canon's basically good control layout
Small and light; carrying around a DSLR can be wearying
Wi-Fi is handy
Fits in the same case as my A1100, which was originally bought for a tiny 35 mm Vivitar I carried as a 2nd camera for years. It's marked "Samsonite World Sport, Model #20" if that helps.

Cons:
Not as good a macro capability as the A1100 (which is sterling at that one thing. I'll be keeping it for that.)
No viewfinder (unlike the A1100. It's not needed all the time, but it is handy)
Slow GPS lock in (my Nexus shows 18 or so satellites in view, and took maybe 30 sec. to lock in. The camera took several times that)
GPS power hog. (It appears to suck up a lot of power, turning it on and off a few times did seem to affect battery charge indication)
No auto bracket (To be fair, that's not common on cameras, but it should be. Canon puts it on the similar S110.)
No hyperfocal distance setting (You can do it manually, of course, but, Canon, why not add another click on the focus bar? There's a computer in there, you know)
Lithium batteries (I prefer the A1100's NiMH AAs so you can get a new set at any Staples for cheap or use alkaline AAs in a pinch)

So, with all of 2 days of experience under my belt:
1) Nice easily-portable camera at a low-ish price
2) Power hog, due to inefficient GPS, big zoom, and powerful microprocessor being pushed by video, etc.
I'll update this review someday when I have some durability information.

Update: 4/27/2014 Took a nice long walk, shot 6 min. of 720p x 30fps video and took 101 L-superfine .jpg (4k x 3k pixel) photos. This used up most of a fully-charged Vivitar 1700 mA-h battery. I got a battery warn and shutdown after my walk while reviewing the video at home. The 1000 mA-h stock Canon battery would give proportionately less life. Canon says that the stock battery is good for 210 photos. A 1700 mA-h Vivitar battery should be good for 147 more than that, or 357 photos. That means that 6 min. of 720p video is worth 256 photos! I don't think anyone will be shooting at 1080p x 60fps much.

Another way to look at it is the number of pixels processed per second by any of the 11 modes of the camera. The normal L .jpg picture takes 12.0E+6 pixels/sec (12 megapixels/sec). The least hungry mode S, takes only 0.307E+6 pixels per second. The hungriest mode is the 14 frames per second L multiple shot mode, which takes 168.E+6 pixels/sec. Since this is only in use for a few frames, it's not bad on battery life. The second worst mode 1080p x 60fps takes 124.E+6 pixels per second, 1037% of the normal L photo processing power! The 720p x 30fps mode I used is only 230% of the normal L mode. Remember, though, the single shot modes are on now and then, maybe a second out of every minute at most. The video modes are on continuously.

NB: Good cameras with a lot of features have historically eaten batteries. I carry around a handful for the A1100.

Misc.: I'm sorry to see the little A1100 get superseded; it was a trouper. Its biggest problem was auto-focusing at long zoom, which isn't a problem if you're taking snapshots in your yard, but it can be a problem if you see a magnificent vista before you. The SX280 shouldn't have a problem with that (manual zoom). YMMV

Update 7/13/2014: My one significant complaint with the SX280 was the macro focusing. As I've gotten more experience with it, some of that has gone away. The SX280's autofocus seems to work differently from the A1100's. I tend to use the macro setting less, and let the normal mode carry the freight, except in extreme cases. In many cases, that's plenty good enough. It's still not as good as the A1100, though. In all other ways, this is an amazing still camera. It also still has too small a battery. Canon seems to be phasing this one out. If you need a still camera and can find one of these cheap, you might consider it.
August, 2017 Update: 3 & a bit years after purchase, the camera is becoming unreliable, throwing E32 (lens) errors more & more frequently. That's not a bad lifespan for a point & shoot, especially with a wide-range zoom lens. The error appears to be focus related.
Sept. 2018 Update: I replaced this with a 720. Much better. I actually cured the lens error with some strong blasts into the lens gaps from canned air. That's risky, blowing dust into the camera, but in this case, it worked. The 280 is now my office camera.
text_fidelity_b: Canon PowerShot SX280 12.1MP Digital Camera with 20x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom with 3-Inch LCD (Black) (OLD MODEL)

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech USB Headset Stereo H650e This is a decent, serviceable headset but rather expensive for the price. I have another Logitech headset for home use but this one was definitely better in quality.

Appearance: the plastic casing feels a little cheap, which raises questions about its durability. I once owned a Sharper Image headphone that had a similar feel, and it broke after a year or so.

Function: the headphone is lightweight and quite comfortable to wear, thanks to the padding on the top and the ear muffs. However, the muffs are thinner than I expected. For the price, I would have liked them to be thicker and offer better noise cancellation capabilities. The microphone, however, feels professional grade, being bendable and sensitive. In addition, the long cord is very work-friendly - it's thicker than conventional cords (preventing easy tangling) and long enough for me to reach over my desk without concern that it'll tug or pop out. Also convenient are the location of the controls for volume, phone and speaker - they're on a rectangular box located on the cord itself. Cool.

However, setting up the headphone took some work. With my other Logitech headphone, all I had to do was plug it into the USB drive, let the computer recognize the device, and off I went. Here, I had to be patient and follow the specific setting instructions for Windows 8. Listening to videos and audio files worked fine, but the microphone function didn't work when my phone rang and I tried ti answer using the mike. I pressed the button but nothing happened. As it turns out, the phone function appears to work only when you're hooked up to Linc, an application that nobody in my office uses. The instructions didn't make this clear.

The sound quality is decent for business purposes but for hi-fidelity sound, it's average. I had assumed it was a noise cancelling headphone because of the padding, but I was wrong - I had no trouble hearing some of my coworkers bickering a few feet away while I was listening to a webinar. I had to up the volume to block them out.

The headphones come with a smooth zippered vinyl pouch for storage or for traveling. This was a very nice touch.

Overall this is a decent enough headphone for work but I would have given it five stars had the price been lower.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech USB Headset Stereo H650e

text_fidelity_a:
Audio-Technica ATH-LS50iSBK In-Ear Monitor Headphones with In-Line Mic & Control, Black These headphones fall between ones I currently own and are, I'd say, a fair price to pay.

In terms of listening to music, they easily out perform standard come-with or cheap earbuds, no doubt about that. So if you're looking to upgrade from that sort and you don't mind the money, it's a no-brainer. They were a bit better than my next step up earphones--more full, more rich, with better base. They fell a little short of my Jaybirds. Again, these have a nice rich sound, but the Jaybirds were crisper, the Audio-Technica ones a bit more muddy.

The fit is excellent. These are very comfortable, the over-the-ear both stable and comfortable--you don't notice it once you're wearing them and they stayed in place nicely while running. They come with a medium size fit, but also come with two smaller sizes.

The microphone worked quite well, people had no trouble hearing or understanding me. I would have liked the control to be adjustable, or a little lower down, but I get why it isn't. Just a personal preference.

So in the end, these seem well priced. They're more expensive than some, but in comparison to those I own that are cheaper than these, the Audio-Technica out-performs them. They don't sound as good as my Jaybirds, but then, they also cost a good amount less, so I wouldn't expect anything different.

In the end, it's you get what you pay for and so it's all up to whether you like to pay for better sound, fit, and comfort. I'm obviously a yes, so I'd say these are worth picking up to replace you're cheaper set.

The light comes with eight lens adapters to cover most of the common applications (49mm, 52mm, 55mm, 58mm, 62mm, 67mm, 72mm, 77mm). The flash offers a continuous light setting, or a flash setting to time with your exposure. You can set it to use all 48 LEDs or just half (can select either the right or the left half).

It’s powered by a battery pack that takes 4AA batteries. The battery contacts on mine were initially out of place and would not make proper contact with the batteries. You can mount the control head on your camera using the hotshoe, or use it off-camera with an included stand. The stand is really light-duty but reasonably functional.

The control head screen is very easy to read. The controls allow for light output brightness adjustments with a simple plus/minus key system, and mode selection (all/half, flash, stead light). There's also a button to test the light output. The buttons are large and well-labeled as to function.

Note that this unit does not allow for delayed/second curtain synch flash.

It includes four diffusers (white, blue, yellow, clear/semi-translucent) that are easy to attach and remove (twist and lift).

I tested this with a Canon 5D mark II and the Canon L 100mm macro and had zero problems with functionality (other than the battery issue listed above).

This is not pro-quality gear but it’s also not pro-level in terms of price. It’s a great way to play around with macro lighting to see if it’s something you find helpful. The all-plastic design keeps this at the 4 star level, but I would certainly recommend it provided you don’t subject it to a lot of heavy use.

Garmin nüvi 1390/1390T 4.3-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I first became enamored of the garmin company after using the one with a rental car. The ease of use and accuracy was impressive. Unfortunately, that model is no longer in production so I opted for this unit.

In general I am pleased. Easy to set up, the unit features a bright, clear screen. It is a snap to use and the directions have been unfailing accurate. I drive alot and so far have used this unit throughout New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, DC and Virginia. I have had no problem with reception even while traversing mountainous regions. I appreciate the advance notice for turns and the voice command system is a convenience.

However, this unit is not flawless. The robotic voice often mispronounces street names and the voice command system seems a bit hard of hearing when it comes to addresses. I have had to pull over and type in the address. The unit does not like to deviate from its chosen route. For instance, one location I frequent in New York is accessible both by the thruway (toll road) and other non-toll main arteries. Both are about the same distance. When I want to avoid the toll route, the unit will recalculate directing that I turn around and follow the initial route multiple times before adjusting to the alternate route. A big deal, no,but annoying nonetheless. While I have not been terribly plagued by the pop ups, they are annoying and potentially unsafe. While the start up guide and manual are adequate, they are barely so. Whatever happened to detailed instructions? But my biggest gripe is the customer service. I called twice with questions and had ridicualously long waits of fifteen minutes and twenty-five minutes respectively. There is no round the clock service. The last time I called it wasnt even available all week, totally unacceptable.

So while I like this system,there is room for improvement.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin nüvi 1390/1390T 4.3-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

The keyboard is not bad, but speed typists would definitely prefer better. Because this is a full-size keyboard, be aware that you'll need ample space on your pull-out keyboard drawer. Some office desks have very narrow and shallow drawers. The mouse is okay too but feels a little cheap. However, this product was obviously not intended to be top-end.

My main criticism of this package is the somewhat confusing owner's manual. Every USB product I've used, particularly a kb or mouse, are plug-and-play. The manual gave instructions for "repairing' with the device, and it was unclear why you would need to issue the series of key commands in order to reconnect via USB on a PC. Perhaps this connection procedure applies only to other types of devices. After one brief failed attempt to connect (see next paragraph), the second try connected okay after I plugged in the USB dongle. I also unplugged/replugged the dongle and it worked again, without having to issue any of the "Esc + K" keypresses that the manual stated were necessary to repair the devices.

I suspect the range of this pairing is not very far. The first time I plugged the dongle in, neither the kb nor the mouse worked. I had to move both closer to the dongle before I got them to connect. The kb and mouse were only four feet from the dongle when I first installed them. After I finally got everything to connect at close range, I moved the kb and mouse back to the distance of four feet, and they continued to work. So I'm not sure of what distance would cause a disconnect.

Linksys WiFi Extender, WiFi 6 Range Booster, Dual-Band Booster, Internet Repeater, 2,000 Sq. ft Coverage, Speeds up to (AX1800) 1.8Gbps - RE7310 You should know up front that this extender only works wirelessly with dual-band WiFi routers (routers with both 2.4GHz and 5GHz).

But it will work as a hard-wired range extender for single-band routers (2.4GHz) using an ethernet cable.

If you have a single band router like we do, it will not detect the wireless network or connect wirelessly. If our neighborhood is any indication, this extender won't work with most home routers. Out of the ten or so visible wireless networks in our area, the extender only detected one or two. The two it detected were two of the weaker signals, but I assume were dual band signals the extender would work with.

After several frustrating attempts to get it connected wirelessly, I spent about an hour with customer support before being informed of this limitation on the extender. The product listing says "compatible with all Wi-Fi routers," and it may be compatible with all routers if set up as a wired extender, but apparently it isn't compatible with all as a wirelessly connected extender. If you want wireless connection to your router, check your router's capability and make sure it is a dual-band router before ordering.

As I mentioned, I did get it set up as a wire-connected extender using an ethernet cable. And it works well for that. It puts a good strong WiFi signal all over our house and much of the yard. I'm giving it four stars for that.

text_fidelity_a:
Moshi AirFoil Screen Protector for Kindle Paperwhite, Kindle, and Kindle Keyboard (2 Pack) Even though I’ve had my various Kindles for years and never gotten a scratch on any of them, I thought it would be nice to have a screen protector so that I could feel more confident throwing my beloved Paperwhite in my purse and taking it on the go. I have also been reading with slightly dirtier hands since I have a new baby, so once again, the screen protector seemed like a good idea to keep it from getting mucked up with drool or whatnot.

The thing that sold me on this particular screen protector is that it makes the claim that it has a permeable surface, so air bubbles don’t get stuck under it during installation. I didn’t find that to be true. Maybe I did something wrong, but I needed to carefully apply it and I used a credit card to apply even pressure to get the bubbles out. Bubbles did not magically disappear nor were they any easier to get out, despite the claim to the contrary.

That said, this is no harder to install than a screen protector on your phone. It’s a bit of a pain, you have to make sure your cats aren’t anywhere nearby, and you have to have meticulously clean hands and very good lighting to make sure you don’t get dust or junk stuck underneath. But once it’s installed, it does exactly what it’s supposed to, and the screen is still very responsive. I really don’t notice it, beyond knowing that my screen is now protected.

Overall, though it doesn’t live up to the hype of being easier to install than other screen protectors, this is a perfectly serviceable product that does what it is supposed to.
text_fidelity_b: Moshi AirFoil Screen Protector for Kindle Paperwhite, Kindle, and Kindle Keyboard (2 Pack)

text_fidelity_a:
Stellar Labs,Outdoor FM Antenna OMNIDIRECTIONAL 9/12/2015
Final Review:
Have now completed the installation and hookup of this antenna. The first test was to listen to Mixed Bag, 90.7 FM which was always full of static. Now this station comes in crystal clear, loud, and strong. Note that I decided to mount this antenna on the side of my house, just beneath the peak of my low roof facing the back yard. I had a quantity of twin 300 ohm cable which I wanted to use. Using a 300ohm/75ohm converter, I simply attached the end of the cable to the two 300ohm screws, protecting the connection with electrical tape. I measured and fabricated a wood mounting plate (see photo) and then screwed the mast bracket to it from the back. The wooden support board was then lag screwed, in turn, to the outside of my house just below the peak using 5" long screws. I then installed the antenna and mast, after reversing it. It now extends upwards vertically yet does not interfere with the roof line. The versatility of the mast permitted me to accomplish that.

(This review is preliminary. I assembled the antenna but am not yet ready to install it.
Assembly tips:

- Both curved antenna segments are secured to the antenna cross bar with the supplied hardware.
- The ends of one (bottom) segment are held in place with two phillips head screws. First, remove the curved metal clamp. line up the holes in the segment and, maintaining hand pressure on each segment end to ensure that it is seated firmly into it's curved metal seat, insert each screw and secure. Do not over tighten these fasteners. This is the "bottom" of the antenna, opposite the 75 ohm connector side. Attach one leg of the segment at a time.
- The ends of the second (top) segment are held in place with two hex head nuts. You will note that each nut is topped with a rubber 'O' ring. This is used to keep the nuts from threading off until assembly. Do not attempt to re-use these as they are not spacers or washers.
- Again, seat the ends of the antenna segment firmly in place, aligning the holes over the studs. Holding down the segment, install each nut. Do not over tighten these nuts.
- The closed loop ends of each antenna segment may now be gently guided in front of the black plastic locking clips. Once the looped ends are in position, firmly, yet carefully snap them into place. The circular antenna shape has now been completed. If assembled patiently and slowly, damage should not occur to the antenna.)
text_fidelity_b: Stellar Labs,Outdoor FM Antenna OMNIDIRECTIONAL

text_fidelity_a:
Toshiba TransMemory Pro USB 3.0 Flash Drive (PFU064U-1BDS) With its huge 64GB file storage capacity, this flash drive can theoretically store the entire contents of a PC's hard drive and its operating system. Since I don't have that many files to store on an everyday basis, I am reserving this flash drive to store high-resolution videos and other RAM-eating monster files.

For $80, this is rather overpriced. There are USB drives that are cheaper and will do the job just as well. To make the USB look like it's worth the extra price, Toshiba made the casing unnecessarily oversized - there's no practical reason why the USB case had to be so wide (you will have trouble sticking another USB drive next to it, which is annoying). It's a gimmick to impress the user, nothing more. However, when you hold it in your hand, it's not as heavy as the metallic finish would lead you to believe - it's actually very lightweight, and to be honest, feels cheap. I have questions of its durability, despite the fancy advertising.

To test, I copied all the videos I had stored in my PC to see how fast it would be to store all of them on this monster drive. I was disappointed that the saving time was not noticeably faster, which may not be the fault of the USB drive but rather my computer. However, I have to say it was a relief that I never got the "you don't have enough memory" message, so you can count on this USB to store tons of videos you can't find room for elsewhere.

The only drawback to this single-USB method of storage is that I don't feel entirely comfortable saving so much stuff on just ONE drive, despite its capacity. It's equivalent to putting all your eggs in one basket - what if you lose that single USB - you're screwed. Though convenient, I'd rather spread out my back-up files, so if you use this USB to save a huge file, I'd buy more than one just to be safe.

The other thing I thought was unnecessary was the included encryption software that's included on the drive. You only see it when you open up the Files folder, and there are two lengthy PDFs with instructions on how to activate the password and security options. Fortunately you do not require to activate them in order to use the drive - I've never found I needed such security measures, but if you plan to store financial data on this USB, it's a good feature.

Lastly, I hate the fact that, unlike my other drives, it has a cap. I am forever losing the caps to my flash drives and have since opted to buy only the retractable ones, where you can slide the connector in or out. Too bad this one doesn't have it, otherwise I would have added a star.

So, in short, a mixed review. Give me a drive that's cheaper, that's big on the inside but small on the outside, capless, and I'd buy more of them.
text_fidelity_b: Toshiba TransMemory Pro USB 3.0 Flash Drive (PFU064U-1BDS)

Allsop Cool Channel Platform LapDesk for Laptop Notebook Computers (29591) I recently purchased a new laptop. Previously, I owned a netbook, and when I used it on my lap, I simply placed it on a couch pillow. Although my new laptop is still small (it's a [[ASIN:B00DEFW6RI Dell XPS Ultrabook/Tablet]]), it is larger than the netbook, and thus I wanted something a bit more stable for lap use. Unfortunately, most of the lap desks I previewed seemed much too bulky for my purposes.

I was very glad to find the Allsop Cool Channel Platform. First, it fits my new 12.5" laptop perfectly, leaving only about 1/2" on either side. Second, the S-curve design hold the laptop at a very comfortable typing angle. Third, my laptop conveniently tucks into the fold of the "S" for storage--this is how I stow it at night, and this is also offers extra protection when I slip the laptop into an external carry case. I also really like the black/gray color and the sturdy, webbed material.

This platform does have a few (minor) drawbacks. When I type on it, there is a bit of wobble to the stand, as it is very lightweight--a plus, but this also means that the surface is less firm. The other slight issue is that the bottom is a bit on the low slide, making it easy for the laptop to slide around. However, as noted, these are quite minor annoyances which have not been overly problematic for me. I would still recommend this stand, with a final rating of 4 1/2 stars.

Logitech 3.5 mm Analog Stereo Headset H151 with Boom Microphone - Black, 7.9"x5.7"x2.4" Good crisp audio quality for phone calls. I like an on-the-ear headset instead of in-ear because cell phones have little or no sidetone.

Don't know what sidetone is? Back in the day, land line phone handsets fed the sound from the mic back into the earpiece, so a person could clearly monitor their own voice (and also hear any other sounds that the other party could hear that the mic picked up). That enabled a person to modulate their own voice (instead of screeching in order to hear themselves) and speak much more clearly. It made for a much better phone conversation experience. That feature was called sidetone.

It's a feature that cell phone designers and engineers somehow decided not to add to cell phones, or to make it so low in volume as to be nonexistent.

So until either cell phone engineers put sidetone back into cell phones or headset manufacturers start building it in as a feature, the workaround is on-ear headsets that allow you to hear your own voice while you speak.

The downside is that on-ear headsets aren't exactly convenient to carry around, and they're not inconspicuous. And they can be a bother if you're wearing a hat.

But they do give you some natural sidetone by allowing you to hear the sound of your voice. And this headset from Logitech, as I said, has some good crisp audio quality for phone calls.

Which brings up another point. Even after years of development, possibly the thing cell phones still do worst is make phone calls. The audio can still be garbled and fluttery due to digitizing and signals that fade in and out in strength. So good audio quality---in that mid-range EQ sweet spot---can make cell phone calls a lot more pleasant.

While there's a volume control on the cord, there's no answer button. That's probably a decision to keep the headset compatible with many devices.

Overall, good headset.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech 3.5 mm Analog Stereo Headset H151 with Boom Microphone - Black, 7.9"x5.7"x2.4"

SanDisk Ultra Fit 128GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - SDCZ43-128G-GAM46 It just landed in the return envelope today... There has been three major things that led to this:
1) The Vault software stopped responding and started crashing every time I tried to run it. Data inside it were obviously inaccessible. So...
2) I decided to make it brand new and reformat the drive. Using just Windows explorer it did not work (refused), then using disk management - no success, finally using prompt and unconditional formatting (both full and quick) would end up in reporting that disk is not accessible - apparently there is writing protection on it that I could not get passed and it would not allow me to reformat it. So...
3) After attempting to reformat the disk became unreadable and Windows could not see it (disk management would see it as raw partition, not able to format it). Next, I took it off the USB port in order to reinsert it and then I almost burned my finger! This thing was so HOT I could fry an egg on it, if it was bigger! After reinserting into the USB port it would still be unrecognizable.
In short, the disk became a small brick and landed in the return envelope.
Avoid SanDisk as they apparently shovel the write protection down your throat and you can't do anything with your drive later on. So much for your customer flexibility with your product. Rather pick a very similar, ultra-small Samsung USB drive of the same size, also available from Amazon. That one comes clean (i.e. no imposed software nor writing protection) and apparently does not heat at all, or very little compared to this little oven.
text_fidelity_b: SanDisk Ultra Fit 128GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - SDCZ43-128G-GAM46

Wyze Cam Outdoor Starter Bundle (Base Station and 1 Cam), 1080p HD Indoor/Outdoor Wire-Free Smart Home Camera with Night Vision, 2-Way Audio, Works with Alexa & Google Assistant, White with Camo Skin Originally, I had a Wyze camera and decided to use it outdoor to watch a duck that nested outside of our front door. Once I got the outdoor covers though, I realized I couldn't make it work. I then bought these 2 outdoor cameras and I am so glad I did. The price and the quality are unbeatable. We have a Ring for our front door. It is good but I think it would not work well for what we are using the cameras for. We have one camera outside hidden monitoring the duck and one put up on the ceiling of our lanai to monitor our pool area where our cat hangs out. She has fallen in the pool several times and we worry about her not being able to get out as she gets older. This camera is amazing. The picture is awesome. The sound would be perfect if we didn't receive some random signal from something else electronic around us. It is as if someone has the same frequency for a radio. However, we really don't need it to have sound or to be able to talk to someone. We want to watch our cat and see when she is at the back door ready to come inside. The one watching the duck has no issues with sound or microphone. The duck actually looks at the camera when you talk to her! :-) We use the share options to let our family watch the duck too! We will use the "duck" cam somewhere else once she has moved on. Very happy I went with these two cameras.

In addition, I didn't use the screws to install either camera. The "duck" cam will be moved eventually and needed to be on the soffit of our house. I obviously do not want holes in the soffit especially when it is not a permanent camera spot. I used an outdoor, double-stick tape by 3M to put it in place. I did this also with the camera for our pool as I didn't want to use screws in the lanai cover. The tape is holding perfectly and the lanai cam will probably stay there with the tape.

The "duck" cam is viewed a lot throughout the day so I would say the battery runs down quickly. The lanai cam is viewed less and I have only a few motion detection settings set up so the battery went down to 17% in a little less than one month. Easy to pop the cam off and charge quickly and then replace it.
text_fidelity_b: Wyze Cam Outdoor Starter Bundle (Base Station and 1 Cam), 1080p HD Indoor/Outdoor Wire-Free Smart Home Camera with Night Vision, 2-Way Audio, Works with Alexa & Google Assistant, White with Camo Skin

text_fidelity_a:
Wireless Keyboard and Mouse Combo, Compact Wireless Keyboard and Mouse Set 2.4G Ultra-Thin Sleek Design for Windows, Computer, Desktop, PC, Notebook, Laptop (Black01) I think this set is very cute in terms of design with some hidden features that is not marketed. So here is what I think.

Build Quality & Design:
I think the color is personal preference, but still think the white-pastel baby pink theme is very cute. Other than that, it doesn't have any unnecessary design element. The finish material is somewhat cheap plastic, but when you consider for $15 keyboard AND mouse set, it is extremely well done. As you can see from photo, they prepared USB-B home on the back, next to battery. Most other companies do that under the mouse, so this was very interesting choice of design. Definitely, it is somewhat inconvenient, if you have to use this set in multiple computer. Other than that, it doesn't bother me at all.

Functionality:
Again, this is somewhat personal preference, this keyboard makes very low hitting sound except the spacebar. I have no idea why they built this way. So it is too much for silence keyboard because of the spacebar but it sounds very dull if you like to hear the mechanical sound of typing. This keyboard doesn't have 6 key island (insert/home/page/delet/end key, normally placed on top of cursor arrows.) If you need for these keys frequently, then this keyboard is not for you. It does have fn-key function so you can use these keys somehow, but it's somewhat inconvenient. Also, they placed backspace twice (one in the conventional place and in the number pad under + sign. This set needs 4 AAA battery, which I think it's a little excessive.

Ergonomics:
Both the keyboard and mouse are very thin, so it feels somewhat inconvenient. Especially the mouse looks and feels very similar to the old apple mouse, adding considerable pressure on wrist. If you are okay with Apple mouse then you will like it. (But not me.)

Buy it if you need : a set of keyboard & mouse with limited budget with extremely cute colors
Don't if you want: ergonomic, full keyboard or if need to use your computer for long time
text_fidelity_b: Wireless Keyboard and Mouse Combo, Compact Wireless Keyboard and Mouse Set 2.4G Ultra-Thin Sleek Design for Windows, Computer, Desktop, PC, Notebook, Laptop (Black01)

text_fidelity_a:
Fitbit Sense 2 Advanced Health and Fitness Smartwatch with Tools to Manage Stress and Sleep, ECG App, SpO2, 24/7 Heart Rate and GPS, Shadow Grey/Graphite, One Size (S & L Bands Included) At this point, I have had the Sense 2 for 2 days and I know at least some of my issues will likely be fixed with later software updates. First, the good. I like the form factor. The case is thin and the watch, even with the supplied band, is comfortable. Speaking of the band, as a big guy, I was overjoyed to see the inclusion of a second band that actually fit. Also, changing bands is a snap.

Overall, it seems to be relatively high quality. The battery life, so far at least has been fantastic. I am on hour 42 of wearing it after a 99% charge and it is down to 70% battery left. The screen is fairly bright and crisp. An understated advantage of the Sense 2 (and one of the reasons I switched) is that is OS and phone brand agnostic. You can use it with Apple or Android and, unlike the Galaxy Watch, there are no features locked away if you are not using the correct brand of phone.

If you are coming from a Galaxy Watch where you could customize the watch face and all sorts of other things and that is important to you, then move along. This watch will not be for you. For now, at least, there is not really much substantive you can do to individualize your user experience. That's not so great.

Also not so great is the things that are missing. There is no Google Maps at launch. Also, despite being a Google company, no support for the Google Assistant (Alexa only sadly). There is also no interface to control music on your phone if that is important to you. I found it mildly annoying, but not a deal breaker. In addition, some people will be turned off by the fact that there are features that require a Fitbit paid subscription to get, even though you get six months for free.

The real reason I bought this watch was the ECG function. I have had A Fib for a couple of years and used to use (and still do) a Kardia XL to check my rhythm. The Galaxy Watch 4 was nice because it did a reasonable single lead reading and it meant not having to carry another gizmo with me. You simply held still and put a finger on each of the side buttons. Unfortunately, when I switched from a Galaxy phone to a Pixel, I lost the ability to do an ECG.

On the Sense 2, the ECG has not been impressive. First, I have big hands and contorting my right one to get my thumb and forefinger on the corner of the glass has been a challenge at time. It often takes several tries to get it right. Second, despite confirming on both my Kardia and my Galaxy Watch, the Sense 2 will never indicate that I am in A Fib. Apparently, if your pulse goes above 120 (which mine frequently does while in A Fib) then the Sense 2 just gives up and won't really check. Even in instances where it was below 120, the Sense will not confirm. I guess we get to settle for inconclusive results instead. Given this feature was the main reason I bought the watch, it may be a deal breaker for me and I may return it for that reason. If this feature is not that important to you, then it may still be a good option.

Overall though, it may be a good option for the right person. If you care primarily about health and fitness tracking and want a good battery life, then this is a good option. At the current $300 price point, I still feel like Fitbit may be asking a little too much given the features of the other higher end options on the market.
text_fidelity_b: Fitbit Sense 2 Advanced Health and Fitness Smartwatch with Tools to Manage Stress and Sleep, ECG App, SpO2, 24/7 Heart Rate and GPS, Shadow Grey/Graphite, One Size (S & L Bands Included)

text_fidelity_a:
APC Back-UPS Pro 1000VA UPS Battery Backup & Surge Protector (BR1000G) I got this for Christmas and have only been using it for a few days now. I did have a problem with the set-up since there were no step by step instructions and you are left to figure out what goes where. I had omitted attaching the USB/phone jack between my old Windows XP computer and the UPS. I've used UPS's in years past, but they did not require a USB connection to a computer. I found out I had a problem when I was trying to install the software and it stopped loading and gave me a problem message, but no solution. I called the 1-888 number and without any fuss or waiting I got to speak to someone in the tech department who spoke very good English and solved my problem quickly.

I was tempted to deduct one star for the lousy (or total lack of) any instructions on how to connect this to your computer but didn't since the tech help was so good. There was a picture drawing instructing the user to remove the battery and turn it over so the green tape is on top which I managed to do alright. I don't hear any fan noise whatsoever as some others were complaining of. In fact, it's so quiet I can't even tell it's on unless I go and see the 3 LED lights on the top panel.

I tested it out a few minutes ago by turning off the power to the room that my computer is in. I was downstairs in the garage at the fuse box so I don't know if any beep occurred upstairs, but when I got there the computer was running off the UPS. Every 30 seconds I heard 4 beeps from the UPS telling me that it was being used as the power source. I only have my computer, monitor and modem connected to the UPS. I figure I don't need the extra peripheral equipment to stay powered up since it only sucks more energy from my UPS. I didn't wait to see how long the UPS would power my PC but I did sit there for about 3 minutes before I went downstairs and turned the power back on. My computer had a message on the screen saying that it was now being powered by regular current again (or something to that effect).

So far I like this UPS a LOT. There's nothing more frustrating then losing your work if the power goes off for only a couple of seconds. I edit a lot of music and it's not always easy or convenient to save it while I edit it just because of the nature of the program I use. So, I really like the idea of hearing my 4 beeps to let me know I might need to close out and shut down and not lose any work. I don't always have lights on so there may be nothing to tell me there's been a power outage except for the beeps on this UPS. There is a mute mode, but I need to hear the beeps.
text_fidelity_b: APC Back-UPS Pro 1000VA UPS Battery Backup & Surge Protector (BR1000G)
